questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2(x+y)-2$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =2(1+1)-2=2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,1) & ={f}_{x}(1,1)(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2(x-1) \\ z-1 & =2x-2 \\ z & =2x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=2x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2x-1$ (or $2x-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨2,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨2,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-2\,k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-2\,k)=i+2\,k$ is also parallel to it.

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,7)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =0+1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-7 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,7)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.
